If we could shrink down to the size of a bacterium and explore the human body
like microscopic adventurers, we would discover something no biology textbook
quite captures: **every part of the body is a different planet**.

The tongue looks nothing like the skin.
The palm of your hand looks nothing like the gut.
And every corner of the body selects, with brutal precision, who gets to live there.

In microbiology, this has a name: **microbial diversity**. And when we measure it
with high-throughput sequencing, the human body stops looking like a uniform
organism and becomes something far more interesting:

::: callout-verde
A planet full of microscopic habitats, each with its own rules,
its own inhabitants, and its own ecological logic.
:::

## 🌍 The body as a collection of ecosystems

Think about the difference between a desert and a tropical rainforest. Both are
on the same planet, but they have different humidity, different temperature,
different nutrients — and completely different organisms adapted to each
environment.

The exact same thing happens inside you.

The **skin of your hands** is a relatively dry environment, exposed to air,
soap, and constant temperature changes. A hostile habitat where only the most
resilient survive — mainly bacteria from the phyla
*Actinobacteriota* and *Proteobacteria*, adapted to arid conditions and high
environmental exposure.

The **tongue**, by contrast, is another story entirely. Constant moisture,
available nutrients, stable temperature, saliva, food remnants and millions of
chemical interactions every minute. Microbiologically speaking, it is a true
tropical rainforest — dominated by *Firmicutes* and with a proportion of
*Fusobacteriota* you won't find anywhere else in the body.

And the **gut** — that great unknown — operates under its own rules:
an anaerobic ecosystem where *Firmicutes* and *Bacteroidota* maintain a
constant balance that affects everything from digestion to immune response.

## 🔬 How we measure the invisible

To quantify these differences we use high-throughput sequencing of the
**16S rRNA gene** (V4 region), the standard molecular marker in microbiome
studies. This gene acts as a biological barcode: each group of bacteria has a
slightly different version, which allows us to identify them without needing
to culture them in the lab.

The analysis pipeline followed the standard **QIIME2** workflow:

```{r pipeline, echo=FALSE}
htmltools::HTML('
<div class="pipeline">
  <span class="pipe-step">Paired-end import</span>
  <span class="pipe-arrow">→</span>
  <span class="pipe-step">DADA2 denoising</span>
  <span class="pipe-arrow">→</span>
  <span class="pipe-step">770 ASVs</span>
  <span class="pipe-arrow">→</span>
  <span class="pipe-step">Silva 138 classification</span>
  <span class="pipe-arrow">→</span>
  <span class="pipe-step">Rarefaction 1,080 reads</span>
  <span class="pipe-arrow">→</span>
  <span class="pipe-step">α / β diversity in R</span>
</div>
')
```

The **DADA2** step is critical: instead of clustering sequences into OTUs at
97% similarity (the classic method), it infers **exact amplicon sequence
variants** (ASVs), resolving single-nucleotide differences. This significantly
reduces false positives and enables cross-study comparisons without losing
taxonomic resolution.

**Rarefaction to 1,080 reads** normalises sequencing depth across samples —
a necessary step to ensure that the diversity differences we observe are
biological, not an artefact of how many reads each sample generated.

## 📊 What we found: a different world at every body site

The starting question was simple: do all body areas harbour similar microbial
communities? The short answer is **no**. The long answer is far more
interesting.

```{r kpis, echo=FALSE}
htmltools::HTML('
<div class="stats-row">
  <div class="stat-card">
    <span class="stat-lbl">Samples analysed</span>
    <span class="stat-val">34</span>
    <span class="stat-sub">2 subjects × 4 sites × time</span>
  </div>
  <div class="stat-card">
    <span class="stat-lbl">Unique ASVs</span>
    <span class="stat-val">770</span>
    <span class="stat-sub">After DADA2 denoising</span>
  </div>
  <div class="stat-card">
    <span class="stat-lbl">Variance explained</span>
    <span class="stat-val">68%</span>
    <span class="stat-sub">PERMANOVA · body site</span>
  </div>
  <div class="stat-card">
    <span class="stat-lbl">Shannon mouth vs skin</span>
    <span class="stat-val">+78%</span>
    <span class="stat-sub">Higher diversity in tongue</span>
  </div>
</div>
')
```

The most striking difference appears when calculating **alpha diversity** —
a measure of how many distinct species coexist in a single sample and how
evenly they are distributed. The Shannon index for the oral cavity (~3.5)
exceeds that of the palms (~2.0) by almost 80%. But that is only the beginning.

When we analyse **beta diversity** — that is, how similar communities are
*between* different samples — the result is even more compelling.
Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity separates
samples almost perfectly by body site. A PERMANOVA test confirms that anatomical
site explains **68% of the total variation in microbial composition**
(R² = 0.68, p = 0.001).

The key finding worth highlighting: **the individual subject explains only 9%**.

In other words: the microbiome of your mouth resembles the mouth of a stranger
more than it resembles your own gut. We are more predictable as a habitat than
as individuals.

::: callout-verde
**Body site matters more than the person.** Anatomy imposes such restrictive
physicochemical conditions that microbial selection converges across different
individuals — regardless of their genetics, diet or lifestyle.
:::

## ⏱️ The microbiome over time: stable or chaotic?

This study has a dimension that cross-sectional analyses cannot capture:
**longitudinal follow-up**. Both subjects were sampled over several months,
making it possible to observe how their microbiome evolves over time.

The gut shows a particularly interesting pattern: despite daily perturbations —
dietary changes, stress, environmental variation — diversity fluctuates but
tends to recover an individual-specific baseline level. This phenomenon is known
as **microbial resilience**, and it is one of the most important concepts in
human microbiome ecology.

We also observed the effect of **antibiotic use**, recorded in the study
metadata. Samples collected during antibiotic treatment show sharp drops in
diversity — a clear ecological perturbation that, in most cases, the system
manages to reverse.

## 👅 The mouth: a microscopic coral reef

The oral cavity deserves special mention. It is not simply "a moist surface"
— it is one of the densest and most dynamic microbial ecosystems in the body,
where bacteria cooperate, compete, form biofilms and exchange genes.

Every meal temporarily alters that environment. Every drink changes the pH.
Every brushing partially reshuffles the community. And yet the ecosystem
manages to remain relatively stable. The characteristic presence of
*Fusobacteriota* — a phylum virtually absent from skin and gut — is such a
clear taxonomic marker that it can identify oral samples from a single look
at phylum-level composition.

## 🧠 Why going beyond "there are bacteria here" matters

The microbiota is no longer studied as a biological curiosity. We know it
influences inflammation, metabolism, immunity and infection. But to understand
that role we first need to answer more basic questions: where are they? how
many are there? how do they change? what perturbs them?

This type of analysis — alpha diversity, beta diversity, taxonomic composition,
longitudinal follow-up, effect of covariates such as antibiotic use — is
the foundation on which more complex clinical studies are built. Without this
scaffolding, correlations between the microbiome and disease lack the ecological
context to stand on.

In the interactive explorer below you can reproduce the analyses,

## ✨ One last thought

Perhaps the most powerful conclusion of this analysis is not statistical.
It is conceptual.

The human body is not a single ecosystem.
It is a collection of microscopic worlds coexisting simultaneously,
each with its own selection rules, its own evolutionary history,
and its own response to perturbations.

The next time you run your tongue over your teeth or rest your hand on a table,
remember: billions of microorganisms just participated in an ecological
interaction that happens constantly — and that we are only beginning to
understand.
